paths.title: Atlantis: every ancient source
paths.description: The story of Atlantis as Plato tells it in the Timaeus and Critias, read on the 9th-century Paris manuscript, followed by every ancient writer who answered him.

steps.heading: Timaeus 22b: "You Greeks are always children"
steps.note: Solon visits the priests of Sais in Egypt, and an old priest tells him the Greeks have no ancient records.

steps.heading: Timaeus 22c: destructions by fire and water
steps.note: Mankind has been destroyed many times, the priest says, and each time the survivors lose their past.

steps.heading: Timaeus 24e: a power from the Atlantic ocean
steps.note: Nine thousand years before Solon, a great host set out from an island beyond the Pillars of Heracles to conquer Europe and Asia.

steps.heading: Timaeus 25d: one grievous day and night
steps.note: Earthquakes and floods: the island of Atlantis is swallowed by the sea and vanishes.

steps.heading: Critias 113c: Poseidon's island
steps.note: Poseidon receives Atlantis as his lot and settles there the children he had with a mortal woman.

steps.heading: Critias 120e-121c: the divine portion fades
steps.note: While the god's nature stayed strong in them they lived nobly; as it was diluted, they grew greedy, and Zeus called the gods together. The dialogue breaks off there.

steps.heading: Strabo 2.3.6: Posidonius on Atlantis
steps.note: The philosopher Posidonius thought the Atlantis story might not be invention, citing real changes of land and sea.

steps.heading: Diodorus 3.56: the Atlantians
steps.note: A people on the shore of the ocean, whose myths of the first gods Diodorus records.

steps.meta: c. 200 AD (citing Theopompus, 4th c. BCE) · Greek · Aelian
steps.heading: Aelian 3.18: the continent beyond the ocean
steps.note: Theopompus' tale of a vast land outside the known world, often read as an answer to Plato.

paths.title: Hyperborea: the land beyond the north wind
paths.description: Every major ancient account of the Hyperboreans, the blessed people of Apollo who lived beyond the north wind, each on its manuscript page.

steps.heading: Pindar, Pythian 10: no road by ship or on foot
steps.note: Neither by ship nor on foot can anyone find the road to the Hyperboreans.

steps.heading: Pindar, Pythian 10: no sickness, no old age
steps.note: They wreathe their hair with golden laurel and feast; no sickness or ruinous old age touches that sacred race.

steps.heading: Pindar, Olympian 3: the olive from the north
steps.note: Heracles brings the wild olive for the Olympic crown from the land of the Hyperboreans.

steps.heading: Herodotus 4.32-36: what is told of the Hyperboreans
steps.note: Herodotus weighs the reports, from Hesiod and Homer to the offerings sent from the north to Delos.

steps.heading: Herodotus 4.13: Aristeas and the one-eyed Arimaspians
steps.note: The poet Aristeas travels north, possessed by Apollo, and hears of the peoples beyond the griffins.

steps.meta: c. 50 BCE (citing Hecataeus, c. 300 BCE) · Greek · Diodorus
steps.heading: Diodorus 2.47: the island and Apollo's round temple
steps.note: An island in the ocean beyond the land of the Celts, birthplace of Leto, with a sacred precinct and a temple of Apollo.

steps.heading: Pausanias 10.5.8: Delphi founded by Hyperboreans
steps.note: The poetess Boeo says the oracle of Delphi was built by men from the Hyperboreans, and that Olen was Apollo's first prophet.

steps.heading: Pliny 4.89: a happy race at the hinge of the world
steps.note: Beyond the Rhipaean mountains, under the pole, with six months of day: a people who live to extreme old age.

steps.heading: Mela 3.36: beyond the Rhipaean mountains
steps.note: The Roman geographer places the Hyperboreans first on the coast of Asia, beyond the Rhipaean mountains, under the north pole (English of Arthur Golding, 1585).

paths.title: The Flood before history
paths.description: The great flood as the oldest written traditions tell it, from the Sumerian king lists to Gilgamesh, Genesis, Enoch and Plato, each on the tablet or manuscript that carries it.

steps.meta: c. 1800 BCE · Sumerian · Sumerian King List
steps.heading: Sumerian King List: kings before the Flood
steps.note: Kingship descends from heaven to Eridu; eight kings reign for 241,200 years, and then the flood sweeps over.

steps.meta: c. 1800 BCE · Sumerian · Sumerian King List
steps.heading: Sumerian King List: after the Flood
steps.note: Kingship descends again, this time to Kish, and the reigns grow shorter.

steps.heading: Eridu Genesis: seven days and seven nights
steps.note: The storms arise together, the flood sweeps the land, and the huge boat is tossed for seven days and nights.

steps.heading: Eridu Genesis: Ziusudra granted life
steps.note: The king who preserved the seed of mankind is given life like a god.

steps.meta: 7th c. BCE tablets · Akkadian · Gilgamesh XI
steps.heading: Gilgamesh XI: "Demolish the house, build a boat"
steps.note: Uta-napishti tells Gilgamesh how the god Ea warned him of the Flood.

steps.meta: 7th c. BCE tablets · Akkadian · Gilgamesh XI (K.3375, the Flood Tablet)
steps.heading: Gilgamesh XI: the dove, the swallow and the raven
steps.note: The boat grounds on Mount Nimush and the birds are sent out, read on the Flood Tablet itself.

steps.heading: Genesis 6: the sons of God and the giants
steps.note: The Nephilim in the earth in those days, and the decision to send the flood.

steps.heading: 1 Enoch 10: Noah is warned
steps.note: Uriel is sent to tell Noah to hide himself; the Watchers who fathered the giants are bound.

paths.title: Becoming like God
paths.description: The ancient sources behind theosis: Plato's "likeness to god", Aristotle's divine life of the mind, the Psalm Jesus quoted, and the Christian promise of the divine nature.

steps.heading: Theaetetus 176b: flight is likeness to god
steps.note: We must fly from here to there as quickly as we can, and to fly is to become like god as far as possible.

steps.heading: Symposium 212a: beauty itself
steps.note: Diotima's ladder ends in the sight of divine beauty; whoever reaches it wins the friendship of heaven and, above all men, is immortal.

steps.heading: Phaedrus 246e-247a: the procession of the gods
steps.note: The souls follow Zeus and the gods to the place beyond heaven.

steps.heading: Aristotle, Ethics 10.7: make ourselves immortal
steps.note: The life of the mind is something divine in us; we should not think mortal thoughts but live by the best thing in us.

steps.meta: 2nd-3rd c. AD (14th c. manuscript) · Greek · Corpus Hermeticum I
steps.heading: Poimandres 26: "to be made one with God"
steps.note: The soul rises through the spheres to the Eighth and into God. This, says Poimandres, is the good end for those who have gained Gnosis: the Greek theothenai means "to be made god", which Mead renders "to be made one with God".

steps.heading: Psalm 82:6: "I have said, Ye are gods"
steps.note: The verse at the root of the theosis debate.

steps.heading: John 10:34: Jesus quotes the Psalm
steps.note: "Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?"

steps.heading: 2 Peter 1:4: partakers of the divine nature
steps.note: The classic scriptural text for theosis, on the page of Codex Sinaiticus.

steps.meta: 4th c. manuscript · Coptic · Gospel of Thomas
steps.heading: Thomas 108: "Whoever drinks from my mouth will become like me"
steps.note: The saying from Nag Hammadi Codex II, line by line on the papyrus.

paths.title: What did Jesus say about divinity?
paths.description: The words attributed to Jesus on the divine nature, followed across Mark, Matthew and John in Codex Sinaiticus, the oldest complete New Testament.

steps.heading: Mark 1:9-11: the baptism
steps.note: The Spirit descends into Jesus and the heavens are torn open.

steps.heading: Matthew 5:48: "Be ye therefore perfect"
steps.note: The command to become teleios, like the Father.

steps.heading: John 1:1-3: "The Word was God"
steps.note: In the beginning was the Logos.

steps.heading: John 10:30-34: "I and my Father are one"; "Ye are gods"
steps.note: Accused of making himself God, Jesus answers with Psalm 82.

steps.heading: John 17:21: "That they all may be one"
steps.note: The prayer that extends divine unity to all believers.

steps.heading: John 1:14: "The Word was made flesh"
steps.note: Divinity enters humanity.
